Dropping terms constant in mm, the per-step cost is f⁡(m)=α​m/2+h/mf(m)=\alpha m/2+h/m with α=λ⁡(k−2​s/L)\alpha=\lambda(k-2s/L), so f′​(m)=α/2−h/m2f^{\prime}(m)=\alpha/2-h/m^{2} and f′′​(m)=2​h/m3f^{\prime\prime}(m)=2h/m^{3}. For h>0h>0 and α>0\alpha>0, ff is strictly convex with minimiser (14), clipped to [1,L][1,L], and a convex function restricted to the divisors of LL is minimised at one of the two divisors that bracket its continuous minimiser. For h>0h>0 and α≤0\alpha\leq 0, ff is decreasing and the minimum is at LL. For h=0h=0, ff is linear and is minimised at an endpoint. Integers that do not divide LL change the objective through the final chunk and are compared through (5). With o>0o>0, (2) gives Δo≈(o/m)​∑i≤m|∂bg⁡(c0+s+k​i,b)|\Delta_{o}\approx(o/m)\sum_{i\leq m}|\partial_{b}g(c_{0}+s+ki,b)| to first order, which is β​o\beta o when the sensitivity is roughly constant at β\beta across the chunk’s loads, a constant per handoff that adds to hh in the first-order condition. ∎

Proposition 2

The objective g0+λ⁡(c0+s+k)+h⁡(s)g_{0}+\lambda(c_{0}+s+k)+h(s) is strictly convex in ss as a sum of a linear and a strictly convex function, so an interior stationary point −h′​(s)=λ-h^{\prime}(s)=\lambda, which exists by hypothesis, is its unique minimiser. ∎

Corollary 2

The first call uses bb and each of the L−1L-1 boundaries reserves o+bg+ov+br=bo+b_{g}+o_{v}+b_{r}=b, so the total is b​LbL even if every retry is used. Splitting a generator failure into undetected and detected cases gives failure probability T⁡(e,qeff,er)T(e,q_{\mathrm{eff}},e_{r}) for each fresh step, hence log-loss ℓv\ell_{v}, and with the additive handoff tax this gives GD,vG_{\mathrm{D},v}. Its advantage over the single agent is Dv​(L)=∑t=2L[g⁡(c0+k​t,b)−ℓv−h]D_{v}(L)=\sum_{t=2}^{L}[g(c_{0}+kt,b)-\ell_{v}-h] with Dv​(1)=0D_{v}(1)=0, whose increments are nondecreasing, so the proof of Theorem 1 applies verbatim. The unverified system with the same summary reservation has fresh-step loss g⁡(cf,b−o)g(c_{f},b-o), so unverified minus verified log-loss is (L−1)​[g⁡(cf,b−o)−ℓv](L-1)[g(c_{f},b-o)-\ell_{v}], which is nonnegative at every depth under the stated condition. ∎

Theorem 5

The indicators are conditionally i.i.d. Bernoulli⁡(1−p)\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-p) given p∼μp\sim\mu by assumption, which gives (15). For fixed p<1/2p<\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} the binomial tail tends to 00, for p>1/2p>\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} to 11, and for p=1/2p=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} to 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, and dominated convergence gives the limit. Under the common-shock law μ=ρ​ε​δ1+ρ⁡(1−ε)​δ0+(1−ρ)​δε\mu=\rho\varepsilon\,\delta_{1}+\rho(1-\varepsilon)\,\delta_{0}+(1-\rho)\,\delta_{\varepsilon}, so the mass above one half is ρ​ε\rho\varepsilon, and (16) follows by conditioning on the shock. Monotonicity in NN for the δε\delta_{\varepsilon} component holds for ε<1/2\varepsilon<\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} and the other components do not depend on NN. Exponential decay at ρ=0\rho=0 is a Chernoff bound. The selector case replaces the majority event by “at least one correct”, which for independent samples has probability 1−εN1-\varepsilon^{N}. ∎

Corollary 3

For conditionally i.i.d. indicators, Cov⁡(Xi,Xj)=Var⁡(p)\mathrm{Cov}(X_{i},X_{j})=\mathrm{Var}(p), so σ2=ρ​ε​(1−ε)\sigma^{2}=\rho\,\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon). Cantelli’s inequality gives μ⁡(p−ε≥t)≤σ2/(σ2+t2)\mu(p-\varepsilon\geq t)\leq\sigma^{2}/(\sigma^{2}+t^{2}) for t>0t>0, and with t=1/2−εt=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}-\varepsilon the left side is μ⁡(p≥1/2)≥F\mu(p\geq\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}})\geq F. Equality in Cantelli holds for the two-point law with atoms at ε+t=1/2\varepsilon+t=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} and ε−σ2/t\varepsilon-\sigma^{2}/t, which is a valid law on [0,1][0,1] iff ε−σ2/t≥0\varepsilon-\sigma^{2}/t\geq 0, i.e. ρ≤(1/2−ε)/(1−ε)\rho\leq(\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}-\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon), and moving the upper atom just above 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} makes FF approach the bound. Theorem 6

By Theorem 5, Evote​(N)→FE_{\mathrm{vote}}(N)\to F. By the saturation hypothesis, ε⁡(c,N​b)→ε∞​(c)\varepsilon(c,Nb)\to\varepsilon_{\infty}(c). If F<ε∞​(c)F<\varepsilon_{\infty}(c) the two limits are separated, so for all large NN the vote failure is below the sequential failure, and symmetrically in the other case. ∎

Appendix B Numerical verification and materials

The closed forms were checked against brute-force evaluation of (4) and (5). Over 200 random draws of (g0,λ,k,s,h,c0)(g_{0},\lambda,k,s,h,c_{0}) with λ∈[10−5,5×10−4]\lambda\in[10^{-5},5\times 10^{-4}], k∈[50,2000]k\in[50,2000], s∈[0,3​k]s\in[0,3k], h∈[0,0.5]h\in[0,0.5], the smallest depth at which D⁡(L)>0D(L)>0 equals (11) on every draw. Corollary 1 was checked exhaustively on all 2,358 combinations of L≤200L\leq 200, m∈{1,2,5,10}m\in\{1,2,5,10\} with m≤Lm\leq L, and h∈{0,0.01,0.1}h\in\{0,0.01,0.1\} at a flat g=0.02g=0.02, remainder chunks included, with no violation. The chunk-size formula agrees with a grid minimiser of the continuous per-step cost to a relative error of 1.7×10−51.7\times 10^{-5} on the 91 of 100 draws with m∗≥1m^{*}\geq 1. Theorem 2 was checked on the saturating curve g(c)=0.2−0.18e−c/10g(c)=0.2-0.18e^{-c/10} with c0=s=0c_{0}=s=0, k=1k=1, and h=0.204h=0.204, where a∞=0.163<h<A∞=1.71a_{\infty}=0.163<h<A_{\infty}=1.71: m=1m=1 never wins within 2,000 steps, and m=2,3,5m=2,3,5 first win at depths 26, 15, and 9 and win at every depth from 28, 17, and 12, since a shorter final chunk can briefly reverse the sign. The identity in its proof matches direct evaluation, including remainder chunks, to within 10−1310^{-13} over 200 random saturating curves. The threshold in Theorem 6 was checked for ε⁡(b)=0.08+0.22​e−b\varepsilon(b)=0.08+0.22e^{-b} at b=1b=1 under the common-shock law: the vote beats the sequential agent at every N∈{3,5,11,51,201}N\in\{3,5,11,51,201\} for ρ∈{0,0.2}\rho\in\{0,0.2\} and loses at every NN for ρ∈{0.5,0.8}\rho\in\{0.5,0.8\}, consistent with ρ∗=0.497\rho^{*}=0.497.

Code and data are at https://github.com/akshitanchan/attention-handoff-tax. The repository contains the verification script, the calibration script (problem generator, filler generator, prompt, grader, resumable runner), the run configuration, the stored responses for all 1,000 pilot calls (final 200 characters each), the per-load summaries, the re-grading script that separates arithmetic from format failures, the script that fits the pilot curve and draws Figure 5, and, for Section 10, the experiment script (ledger generator, both runners, the handoff-tax runner, the analysis), the per-step records for all 40,600 calls with finish reasons and token counts, the run configurations, the initial analysis output, and the exposure-matched analysis of Section 10 with its bootstrap and sensitivity runs. For the pilot, the serving stack was Ollama 0.30.8 with the packaged gpt-oss:20b model (Ollama ID 17052f91a42e, 20.9B parameters, MXFP4) behind a derived model with a 71,680-token window (ID eec2acdf0143). The ollama show and ollama list output, captured when the files were assembled, is included with the run configuration.

Use of AI tools.

The authors directed the research and conducted all experiments. AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT) were used as supplementary tools for checking and writing assistance. All results and claims were independently verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the work.
